name: Coined money
note: Standardised metal coins as medium of exchange and store of value are already well established practice across the literate ancient world by this date.

name: Deposit bankers (argentarii)
note: Money changers and deposit takers, attested across the ancient world (Rome's argentarii are the best-documented case): accept deposits, testify to witnesses about amounts held, but do not yet systematically lend.

name: Maritime loan at high interest
note: High-interest loan for sea trade, forgiven if cargo is lost to weather. The lender bears the ship loss risk, the high interest compensates.

name: Partnership (societas)
note: Contractual partnership between two or more parties to share profits and losses. Legally recognised, but partners remain personally liable.

name: Testament and inheritance law
note: Formal document disposing of property at death. Creates certainty and allows wealth to be controlled across generations.

name: Contract law and enforcement
note: Legal framework for enforcing voluntary agreements. Necessary foundation for all complex commerce.

name: Tax farming and revenue contracts
note: State contracts out tax collection to private businessmen. Transfers risk to the contractor in exchange for immediate cash.

name: Permanent market and market law
note: Regular marketplace with established location, rules, and enforcement. Reduces search costs for buyers and sellers.

name: Auction and competitive bidding
note: Sale to highest bidder, used for slaves, real estate, and state contracts. Reveals market value and discourages corruption.

name: Annona grain dole and administration
note: State purchase and distribution of grain. Requires contracts with producers, shipping, storage, and accounting.

name: Professional associations (collegia)
note: Craft guilds and professional societies. Enforce standards, restrict entry, and provide mutual aid. State views them with suspicion.

name: Arabic numerals in commerce
note: Position notation with zero makes arithmetic dramatically faster than the tally, rod or numeral systems it replaces (Roman numerals among them). Merchants who adopt it can calculate faster than competitors, reducing error and increasing profit.

name: Double-entry bookkeeping
note: Every transaction appears twice, once as debit, once as credit. Makes error self-detecting: if debit total does not equal credit total, there is an arithmetic mistake. This is the foundation of trust between owner and manager across distance. Without it, the manager can simply lie.

name: Ledger and account books
note: Permanent record of all accounts, organised by account type. Enables consistent accounting over years and allows auditing.

name: Trial balance and error detection
note: Periodic total of all accounts to verify that debits equal credits. Catches errors before they propagate and corrupt future records.

name: Bill of exchange
note: A transferable written order settles a distant debt through a trusted merchant and banking network. The project is network acceptance and repeated clearing, not merely writing one document.

name: Endorsement and negotiability
note: The holder can sign the back of a bill and pass it to another party. Transforms a personal IOU into a negotiable instrument that can be traded like currency.

name: Cheque and demand draft
note: Demand draft on a bank, payable on sight. Unlike a bill of exchange, it is not a promise to pay at a future date but an order to transfer immediately from the drawer's deposit.

name: Promissory note
note: Promise by one party to pay a fixed sum to another at a future date. Simpler than a bill of exchange and does not require a third party.

name: Discounting and advance payment
note: A banker buys a future payment at a discount, paying less than the face value today. The difference is the interest charge. Transforms future cash into immediate liquidity.

name: Deposit bank and current account
note: Bank that accepts deposits and allows withdrawal on demand. Not merely storage but active management of customer funds. Requires trust, double-entry records, and systematic procedures.

name: Fractional reserve banking
note: Bank lends out most of the deposits it receives, keeping only a fraction in reserve. Multiplies the money supply and increases lending capacity but creates risk if too many depositors demand withdrawal at once.

name: Clearing house and interbank settlement
note: Central place where multiple banks settle debts to each other by netting. A merchant from bank A pays a merchant from bank B thousands of times per day. Instead of settling each individually, the clearing house nets all transactions and banks owe each other only the balance.

name: Joint-stock company with permanent existence
note: Business owned by many shareholders, each owning a fixed fraction. Survives the death of any owner. Allows raising capital from people who do not want to be personally involved in management. Competes directly with the family business model.

name: Limited liability
note: Shareholder loses only the money invested, not personal assets. Not a tax dodge. This is what makes a stranger willing to invest in a ship or factory he cannot supervise. Without it, any disaster bankrupts him and he avoids the risk entirely.

name: Share and share transfer
note: Transferable ownership certificate. Shareholder can sell to another without dissolving the company. Makes capital liquid and allows investment without long commitment.

name: Stock exchange and organised trading
note: Permanent marketplace for shares. Allows quick price discovery and liquid exit. Draws wealth from direct business operations into financial markets.

name: Bond and debt security
note: Fixed-income security representing a debt obligation. Pays coupons on schedule and returns principal at maturity. Tradeable like shares.

name: Public debt and government borrowing
note: State borrows money instead of raising taxes or debasing currency. A state that can borrow can survive temporary deficits and invest in long-term projects without waiting for revenue. A state that cannot borrow must tax harder or debase, both politically costly.

name: Central bank and monetary authority
note: Bank chartered by the state to manage the nation's monetary system. Acts as lender of last resort and regulates other banks. Threatens existing banking families with monopoly loss.

name: Paper money and note issue
note: Central bank issues paper notes redeemable in metal on demand. Solves the portability problem of coined money but introduces counterfeiting risk and requires trust in the issuer.

name: Seigniorage and debasement
note: Profit from issuing new money, the difference between the value of the coin and the value of the metal in it. Tempts rulers to debase currency by reducing metal content. Short-term profit destroys long-term monetary trust.

name: Bimetallism and fixed exchange
note: Fix a legal ratio of gold to silver coins. Solves the problem of scarce gold by allowing silver to serve as backup. But if the market ratio diverges from the fixed ratio, people hoard the undervalued metal.

name: Marine insurance
note: A premium-for-indemnity contract transfers the risk of a specified cargo or vessel loss to underwriters. The project is not discovering risk: it establishes standard policies, shared loss records, underwriting practice, reserves, and enforceable claims among existing bankers and maritime lenders.

name: Fire insurance
note: Insurance against fire loss of buildings and goods. Solves the problem of catastrophic unexpected loss. Insurers must pool many risks so that a single event does not bankrupt them.

name: Life insurance
note: Insurance against death, paying a benefit to the beneficiary. Requires mortality data to price correctly. Allows families to insure against the death of breadwinners.

name: Mortality table and actuarial mathematics
note: Systematic data on age at death, allowing calculation of the probability of death at each age. Without this, life insurance premiums are guesses. With it, they are calculated.

name: Reinsurance and risk pooling
note: Insurance for insurance companies. An insurer buys reinsurance to protect against catastrophic losses. Allows insurers to take on larger risks than their own capital supports.

name: Mortgage and real estate credit
note: Loan secured by real estate, which can be seized if the borrower defaults. Allows the poor to buy land by spreading payment over years.

name: Annuity and fixed income stream
note: Contract paying a fixed income for life or a fixed term. Allows the elderly to convert a lump sum into regular payments. Requires good mortality data to price.

name: Pension and retirement scheme
note: Employer or state commits to paying workers income after retirement. Requires huge capital accumulation and actuarial discipline. Creates obligation that survives the employer.

name: Savings bank for small deposits
note: Bank accepting small deposits from poor people and paying interest. Encourages thrift and provides safe storage. Rare because the overhead of managing thousands of small accounts is high.

name: Pawnshop and secured loan
note: Loan in exchange for movable goods as security. If not repaid, the pawnbroker sells the goods. Often the only credit available to the poor. Profits from high interest and sale of forfeited items.

name: Usury law and interest regulation
note: Legal limit on interest rates. Prevents exploitation of desperate borrowers but suppresses lending because lenders cannot be compensated for risk. Regularly evaded through fiction.

name: Usury evasion through legal fiction
note: Structure a loan as sale with buyback, or as a partnership, to hide the interest. If caught, the lender loses everything and may be punished. Ubiquitous despite the risk.

name: Bankruptcy law and insolvency
note: Legal process when a debtor cannot pay. Creditors receive a fraction of their claims. Without it, a debtor can simply flee or hide assets. With it, creditors have incentive to give credit in the first place.

name: Patent and exclusive right
note: A state-recognised registry grants a time-limited exclusive right in exchange for public disclosure. An inventor can petition immediately, but completion means recognition and enforcement by the state.

name: Patent office and examination
note: Government body that examines patent applications for novelty and issues letters patent. Requires technical expertise and creates a complete archive of inventions.

name: Copyright and literary rights
note: Exclusive right to copy a book or written work for a limited time. Gives authors incentive to publish but restricts who can make copies. Requires printing to be valuable.

name: Trademark and mark of quality
note: A public registry records a maker mark and a court enforces it against confusing use. Ancient maker marks need no invention; the project is the registry and enforceable exclusive right.

name: Brand and goodwill
note: Reputation for quality associated with a maker's mark. Allows the maker to charge premium prices and is valuable enough to be sold separately from the business.

name: Contract of employment
note: Written agreement specifying duties, term, and compensation. Protects both employer and employee and reduces disputes.

name: Wage and labour payment
note: Regular payment for labour, in coin or in kind, wherever a cash or barter economy already exists.

name: Company town and tied housing
note: Employer provides housing, food, and goods to workers in a closed economy. Workers cannot leave without losing housing and may be paid in company scrip. Highly profitable but politically dangerous.

name: Trade union and workers collegium
note: A workers collegium organised for collective bargaining rather than social worship alone. Because Roman authorities police associations as potential factions, recognition and protection are the central project.

name: Cartel and market sharing agreement
note: A monitored agreement among established sellers to allocate customers, territory, or output. Its difficulty is repeated enforcement among rivals, not inventing private collusion.

name: Monopoly and exclusive grant
note: State grants exclusive right to sell a good. Raises prices but guarantees supply. Often granted to extract more tax. Breaks existing merchants' ability to compete.

name: Tariff and import duty
note: Tax on imported goods. Raises revenue and protects local producers from foreign competition. Typically unpopular with consumers.

name: Customs house and tariff collection
note: Office at border or port to assess and collect tariffs. Inspectors examine goods to determine their nature and value. Requires clerical staff and standardised procedures.

name: Standard weights and measures
note: Approved standard measures held by the state and enforced in markets. Prevents fraud and allows price comparison across merchants and time.

name: Assay office and hallmarking
note: Official test of precious metal fineness, with a hallmark proving the state's guarantee. Allows buyers to trust the quality without testing every item.

name: Futures contract and forward dealing
note: Agreement to buy or sell a commodity at a fixed price on a future date. Allows farmers to lock in a price and speculators to bet on price changes. Subject to default risk.

name: Commodity exchange and standardised contracts
note: Market for standardised futures contracts, allowing rapid trading and price discovery. Grading systems ensure all contracts for a good are actually equivalent.

name: Arbitrage and price equalisation
note: Buy cheap in one place and sell dear in another. Requires quick transport and communication. Drives prices toward equilibrium across locations and is profitable only when markets are fragmented.

name: Newspaper as business and subscription
note: Regular publication reporting news, sold by subscription or single copy. Profitable from subscriptions and later advertising. Attracts literacy and creates information market.

name: Advertising as industry
note: Merchants pay to announce their goods in newspapers and on placards. Becomes major revenue source for publishers. Creates a market for attention.

name: Classified advertisement
note: Small notice for sale or hire of specific items. Much cheaper than display advertising and highly profitable because readers actively search for them.

name: Almanac and reference publication
note: Annual publication of tables, calendars, and reference data. Farmers, sailors, and merchants each buy the relevant sections. Popular and profitable.

name: Directory and business listing
note: Alphabetical listing of merchants, trades, and professions in a city with addresses. Reduces search costs for consumers. Sellers pay to list themselves.

name: Postal service as paid business
note: A private, paid relay for letters and small parcels, adapted from an existing courier network. Contracts define custody and liability; inns provide public staging points, while scheduled riders, replacement horses, route agents, and delivery records make service reliable enough for merchants to buy.

name: Post office and mail handling
note: Office receiving, sorting, and forwarding mail. Centralises handling and creates accountability. Prevents loss and enables tracking.

name: Postage stamp and paid marking
note: Adhesive mark proving postage paid. Replaced trust in the post office with prepaid proof. Enables sender to pay instead of recipient.

name: Telegraph as commercial service
note: Companies operate telegraph networks and sell message transmission by the word. Enables rapid long-distance communication of prices and news.

name: News agency and wire service
note: Service collecting news from correspondents and selling it to newspapers via telegraph. Reduces cost of news gathering and allows small papers to compete.

name: Lending library and subscription library
note: Members pay subscription fee to borrow books. Economical because each book is read by many people. Profitable even if each book costs more than any individual would pay.

name: Coffee house as information market
note: Establishment where customers gather to drink coffee and exchange information. Merchants trade information about prices, shipments, and credit. Newspapers available. Becomes centre of financial gossip.

name: Theatre as business
note: Turn an existing theatre tradition into a regular admission-charging business. The project establishes performance contracts, ticketing, scheduled programmes, concessions, and accounts; it changes a patronage- and festival-led institution into a repeat commercial operation. A theatre, not an amphitheatre, is the relevant venue.

name: Printed playing card and card game
note: Woodcut cards, faster and cheaper than hand-painted. Creates mass market for cards. High profit because cards wear out and players buy replacements.

name: Gambling house and gaming establishment
note: Establishment where customers gamble, with the house taking a cut of all winnings. Highly profitable but attracts violence and is often banned or heavily taxed.

name: Public revenue lottery
note: A government-authorised sale of numbered chances funds a declared public purpose, with published drawing and payout rules. Private lots and prize distributions are ancient; the reform is a recurring revenue-raising institution.

name: Racecourse and pari-mutuel betting
note: Operate pooled betting at an existing horse-racing circus. Stakes on each outcome form a pool; after the operator takes a published percentage, winning tickets divide the balance. The project establishes tickets, closing rules, accounting, settlement, and controls against altered entries rather than pretending to invent Roman racing.

name: Totalisator machine and automated payout
note: Machine that collects bets, calculates odds, and prints tickets. Allows rapid handling of high volume. Can calculate complex betting combinations automatically.

name: Professional sport as business
note: Athletes paid to compete in front of paying audiences. Ticket sales, concessions, and gambling generate revenue. Creates a career outside traditional trades.

name: Ferry and toll crossing
note: Regular boat crossing operated for a fee. Operator owns boat and landing and extracts rent from every crossing. Profitable if there is no alternative.

name: Toll bridge and road toll
note: Operator builds or repairs a bridge and collects tolls from every user. High initial cost but profitable over decades. Reduces journey time compared to fording.

name: Turnpike trust and road company
note: Company builds high-quality toll road, collecting tolls to repay investment and fund maintenance. Significantly faster travel time attracts commercial traffic.

name: Canal company and inland waterway
note: Company digs canal and charges tolls for passage. Massive investment but water transport is cheaper than land transport for bulk goods. Attracts industries that use water.

name: Railway company and rail service
note: Company operates railroad and charges passengers and freight shippers. Transforms inland transportation but requires massive capital investment and creates monopoly power.

name: Tramway and urban rail
note: Streetcar line within a city, powered by horse or later electricity. Charges passengers and concentrates development along the line.

name: Omnibus and public stage coach
note: Coach carrying multiple paying passengers on a fixed route. Cheaper than hiring a private carriage. Operates on schedule and shares capacity with strangers.

name: Hotel and commercial lodging
note: A larger urban lodging house rents multiple rooms and coordinates meals, servants, storage, and longer stays under one proprietor. Roman hospitia and substantial medieval hostelries distinguish this from the smaller tavern-inn; the commercial practice can be inherited even though an individual establishment still requires capital.

name: Inn and coaching house
note: A small commercial lodging house sells travellers a bed, food, drink, and often stabling. Roman cauponae and tabernae, Norse roadside or port hospitality, and later medieval inns differ in law and architecture but share this inherited operating practice; an individual premises still requires ordinary capital.

name: Restaurant and commercial kitchen
note: Establishment serving prepared meals to paying customers. Separate from lodging. Requires reliable supply of ingredients and skilled cooks.

name: Department store and general merchandise
note: Single building selling multiple categories of goods under one roof. Reduces customer search time and allows operators to manage inventory centrally.

name: Mail order catalogue and distance selling
note: Company publishes catalogue and sends it to customers nationwide. Orders arrive by post and goods ship via mail or carrier. Enables shopping without a store visit.

name: Chain store and multiple locations
note: Company operates identical stores in multiple cities, buying centrally and selling retail in each location. Achieves scale but requires sophisticated management and accounting.

name: Trading post and remote store
note: Store in remote area, often far from competition. High margins because goods are rare locally but operator faces transportation cost and risk.

name: Factory and integrated production
note: Single building housing all production steps, with standardised procedures and division of labour. Dramatically increases output per worker and reduces defects.

name: Plantation and large estate agriculture
note: A large market-oriented estate coordinates specialised crop production and a substantial tenant, bound, enslaved, or wage workforce. Roman latifundia and medieval demesnes are inherited forms; later colonial plantations are more specialised and coercive variants, not the invention of large-estate management.

name: Guild and monopoly craft
note: A licensed craft association that controls entry, training, and market privileges. It builds on an existing collegium but requires political recognition for monopoly powers.

name: Apprenticeship indenture and training contract
note: Written contract binding a youth to a master for learning a trade, usually 7 years. Controls training standards and succession but binds the apprentice to one employer.

name: Professional examination and licence
note: State or guild administers written or practical test to certify competence. Prevents unqualified practitioners from harming customers. Restricts entry but creates credible certification.

name: University and degree-granting institution
note: School awarding degrees that certify learning. Charges tuition but also grants scholarships. Attracts scholars and students and creates local employment.

name: Endowed chair and endowment
note: Wealthy patron donates capital and the income is used to pay a professor. Removes the chair from student fees and allows focus on scholarship rather than teaching revenue.

name: Research institute and endowed laboratory
note: Institute funded by endowment, focused purely on research without teaching obligation. Attracts top scholars and creates knowledge spillovers to industry.

name: Learned society and academic journal
note: Society of scholars publishing a regular journal of discoveries. Creates peer review and credibility. Charges subscription and creates career incentive for scholars to publish.

name: Museum and public collection
note: Building housing collections of art, specimens, and antiquities open to the public. Charges admission and attracts tourism. Requires space, climate control, and security.

name: Census and population enumeration
note: Official counting of population by age, sex, occupation, and wealth. Enables taxation and conscription and produces economic data. Expensive but government views it as essential.

name: Survey and map as state instrument
note: Government surveys territory systematically and produces maps. Used for tax assessment, military planning, and engineering projects. Creates baseline for all future development.

name: Standing bureaucracy
note: Professional staff of administrators employed by the state to carry out government functions. Any society with meaningful state capacity already has some version of this.

name: Civil service examination
note: Competitive written examination for appointment to government positions. Replaces patronage with merit, reducing corruption and improving quality of administration.

name: Statistical office and data collection
note: Office that collects, compiles, and publishes data on trade, prices, production, and population. Enables policy decisions based on facts rather than anecdote.
